---
title: "Solutions: Linear regression"
---

::: {.callout-note}
These are the solutions to the
[Linear regression](../lecture-02/04-linear-regression.qmd) exercises.
Try each exercise yourself before you look.
:::

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(medicaldata)
```

`opt_clean`, made at the top of the Linear regression page:

```{r}
opt_clean <- opt |>
  mutate(
    Birth.outcome = str_trim(Birth.outcome),
    Group = factor(Group, levels = c("C", "T"),
                   labels = c("control", "treatment"))
  ) |>
  filter(Birth.outcome == "Live birth") |>
  select(PID, Clinic, Group, Age, BMI, Birthweight, GA.at.outcome)
```

## Exercise 1: Fit a linear regression

```{r}
ggplot(opt_clean, aes(x = Group, y = Birthweight)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "Group", y = "Birth weight (g)")
```

**(1)** The two groups look almost the same,
with a long tail of very light babies in both.

```{r}
bw_fit <- linear_reg() |>
  fit(Birthweight ~ Group, data = opt_clean)

bw_tidy <- tidy(bw_fit, conf.int = TRUE)
bw_tidy
```

**(3)** The intercept, `r round(bw_tidy$estimate[1])` g,
is the control group's mean birth weight.

**(4)** The treatment coefficient, `r round(bw_tidy$estimate[2])` g,
is the difference between the treatment and control means.

**(5)** Its 95% confidence interval,
`r round(bw_tidy$conf.low[2])` to `r round(bw_tidy$conf.high[2])` g,
includes 0 (p = `r signif(bw_tidy$p.value[2], 2)`),
so we have no evidence that the treatment changed birth weight.

The group means show where the intercept and the treatment coefficient come from:

```{r}
opt_clean |>
  group_by(Group) |>
  summarize(n = n(), mean_birthweight = mean(Birthweight))
```
